captions:
Every time you push code, something could happen
automatically.
Tests could run. A build could ship. A bug
could be caught before anyone sees it.

That something is GitHub Actions. Let's learn it
from
zero to production — and then tour the rest
of GitHub.
Picture a team with no automation.
A developer finishes a feature. Now they run the
tests by hand — if they remember. They build
the app on their own laptop. They copy files
to a server.
Then comes the classic line: it works on my
machine.
Every step is slow, manual, and easy to get
wrong. And it happens dozens of times a day,
across the whole team.

Now picture a robot that watches your repository.
The
moment code arrives, it runs every step, the same
way, every time, on a clean machine.
That robot is what we're building toward.
GitHub Actions isn't new, but it has grown fast.

It was announced in twenty eighteen, and became
generally
available with full CI/CD in late twenty nineteen.

Since then it has added keyless cloud logins,
reusable

workflows, Arm runners, and signed build
attestations.

In January twenty twenty six, GitHub cut hosted
runner
prices by up to thirty nine percent.
Today it's the default automation engine for a huge
share of projects on GitHub — and for public

open source repositories, standard runners are
completely free.
Here's the map.
We start with the big picture, then the anatomy
of a workflow file, line by line.

Then triggers, runners and jobs, and the reusable
actions
that make it all fast.

Next, how data flows — expressions, secrets, outputs
and
caching.

Then deployments, security, cost, speed and
debugging.
And finally, a tour of the rest of GitHub

— pull requests, issues, projects, Codespaces,
Copilot and security
features.
By the end, you'll read any workflow file, and
write your own.
